claims.claim: Coagulopath, quoted by nostalgebraist, describes R1's overwhelming reliance on cliche as spinning a Rolodex of 20-30 generic images and selecting one at random.
claims.source: Coagulopath, commenter, quoted verbatim by nostalgebraist on Tumblr, March 2025
claims.quote: spinning its Rolodex of 20-30 generic images

claims.feature: other: no idle detail (everything is functional)
claims.claim: Coagulopath, quoted by nostalgebraist, complains that in R1 fiction every line of dialogue advances the plot and every description is functional, so nothing on the page has weight.
claims.source: Coagulopath, commenter, quoted verbatim by nostalgebraist on Tumblr, March 2025
claims.quote: Every line of dialog advances the plot

claims.claim: Coagulopath, quoted by nostalgebraist, reports that reprompting R1 after a story you dislike is almost pointless because you just get the same stuff again.
claims.source: Coagulopath, commenter, quoted verbatim by nostalgebraist on Tumblr, March 2025
claims.quote: you just get the same stuff again

claims.claim: Guo lists monotony as a tell, writing that in AI-generated content sentences are roughly the same length and the cadence never varies.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: Sentences are roughly the same length

claims.claim: Guo observes that LLMs uncommonly switch person or tense and tend to pick a lane and stay in it with unnatural consistency.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: They tend to pick a lane and stay in it

claims.claim: Guo argues that AI metaphors are plausible and generic, gesturing toward meaning without quite achieving it, whereas human metaphors are either highly specific or culturally resonant.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: They gesture toward meaning without quite achieving it

claims.feature: other: surface polish with nothing underneath
claims.claim: Guo names the combination of surface polish with nothing underneath as AI's signature failure.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025

claims.claim: Guo reports that a common AI failure is a paragraph saying in four sentences something that could easily have been said in one, with the other three adding nothing.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: in four sentences something that could easily have been said

claims.claim: Guo rejects absence of typos as a tell, writing that with tools like Grammarly widespread, perfect grammar is no longer the smoking gun it once was.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: Perfect grammar is no longer the smoking gun it once was

claims.feature: other: frequency not presence is the tell
claims.claim: Guo argues that the devices themselves are not the difference: a good writer uses these devices sparingly and with intention, while AI litters them throughout its writing indiscriminately.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: a good writer uses these devices sparingly, and with intention

claims.claim: Guo states that AI writing detectors do not work and produce false positives at alarming rates.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: They produce false positives at alarming rates

claims.claim: Guo says his own defence against AI slop is to cultivate specificity, writing things rooted in particular knowledge and tangible experience, which he says AI still struggles to replicate convincingly.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: to write things rooted in particular knowledge and tangible experience

claims.claim: Guo reports anecdotally that GPT-4o produces emoji-led bullet lists more than its predecessors and, anecdotally, more than GPT-5, and that he rarely sees Claude do it.
claims.source: Charlie Guo, Artificial Ignorance newsletter, 22 October 2025
claims.quote: GPT-4o does this more than its predecessors

claims.claim: Scalzi wrote in February 2023 that the AI-generated stories then flooding science fiction magazines are kinda trash.
claims.quote: all these generated stories are kinda trash

claims.claim: Scalzi argues that a single prompter sees one output and may find it original, but an editor sees the current AI tropes dozens of times with each new iteration of the generators.
claims.quote: see the current AI tropes dozens of times
claims.page: para. beginning "If this is indeed mostly scamsters"
